message.content:
The lion (Panthera leo) and the zebra (Equus zebra) diverge far back in mammalian history.  
Their most recent common ancestor is the last common ancestor of the clade **Laurasiatheria** – the group that contains both the order Carnivora (cats, dogs, bears, etc.) and the order Perissodactyla (horses, zebras, rhinos).  

That ancestor was a small, insect‑eating mammal that lived roughly 70–80 million years ago, long before the diversification of the modern carnivores and odd‑toed ungulates. There is no living species that corresponds to it; it is a hypothetical, extinct ancestor inferred from comparative anatomy and molecular phylogenetics.

Lion is a big cat (Panthera leo), zebra is a horse family (Equus zebra). Both are mammals, but more specifically both are in the order Carnivora (lion) and Perissodactyla (zebra). They share a common ancestor at some level. The common ancestor of lion and zebra would be the last common ancestor of the two species. That would be the last common ancestor of the families Felidae and Equidae. That ancestor would be a mammal from the order of placental mammals, maybe the last common ancestor of the clade that includes both Carnivora and Perissodactyla. That would be the last common ancestor of the clade that includes all perissodactyls and carnivorans, which is the clade of Laurasiatheria? Actually, Carnivora and Perissodactyla are both part of the clade Laurasiatheria. So the last common ancestor of lion and zebra would be the last common ancestor of the Laurasiatheria clade. That ancestor would be a mammal that lived around 70-80 million years ago. It might be a small, insectivorous mammal. But the question likely expects "the last common ancestor of the clade Laurasiatheria" or "the last common ancestor of the clade that includes both Carnivora and Perissodactyla." Or maybe they want "the last common ancestor of the clade that includes all placental mammals" which is older. But the question: "What is the common ancestor of lion and zebra?" The answer: "The last common ancestor of the clade Laurasiatheria, which lived about 70-80 million years ago." Or "the last common ancestor of the clade that includes both Carnivora and Perissodactyla." So we can answer that. There's no specific species name. It's a hypothetical ancestor. So we can say: "The last common ancestor of the clade Laurasiatheria, a small, insectivorous mammal that lived around 70-80 million years ago." That is the answer. No tool needed.
